pos: n. (the kingdom broken in three at Mohacs, where the Reformation spread through the ruin and the Reformed church became the church of the Magyars)
etymology: Latin Hungaria, from the Onogur confederacy; Hungarian Magyarország, the land of the Magyars.
biblical_def: Hungary is the kingdom in which the Reformation advanced because the state collapsed. The Ottoman victory at Mohacs in 1526 killed the king and most of the bishops and split the realm into three: Royal Hungary under the Habsburgs in the west and north, the central plain under Ottoman administration, and the principality of Transylvania in the east. In the Ottoman zone the Catholic hierarchy simply ceased to function, and Reformed preaching filled the vacuum almost unopposed, the Turks caring nothing which sort of Christian paid the tax. The Germans and Slovaks of the northern towns took the Augsburg Confession; the Magyars took the Helvetic, and the Synod of Debrecen in 1567 adopted the Second Helvetic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism for the Hungarian Reformed church. Gaspar Karoli's complete Hungarian Bible was printed at Vizsoly in 1590 and remains the Hungarian Protestant Bible. The Habsburg counter-reformation under Peter Pazmany and his successors recovered the magnates by patronage and the towns by force; the Peace of Vienna of 1606, won by Bocskai's revolt, and the Diet of Linz of 1645 secured legal standing, and the Decade of Mourning from 1671 took it away again. The dictionary enters Hungary because its Reformed church was built in a ruined state, with no king's help at any point, and outlasted the empires on both sides of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a diet as an assembly of princes or estates; a confession as a formulary of articles of faith; a magnate as a person of rank; and tribute as a sum paid by one prince to another.
webster_full: DIET, n. An assembly of the states or circles of the empire; a convention of princes and delegates.
CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a profession of belief.
MAGNATE, n. A person of rank; a grandee or noble; a man of great power or influence.
TRIBUTE, n. An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one prince or nation to another.
VACANCY, n. Empty space; vacuity; a place or office unoccupied.

Act 2:8

corruption_summary: The kingdom split in three after Mohacs in 1526, where Reformed preaching filled the collapse and the Synod of Debrecen settled the Hungarian church in 1567.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the assumption that the gospel needs a friendly state to advance, which Hungary refutes from both directions. Under the Turk there was no Christian magistrate at all, and the Reformed church grew fastest; under the Habsburg there was a Christian magistrate who used his office against it, and it grew slowest. What actually advanced it was preachers sent out and congregations taught in Hungarian. “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) is the question whose answer built the Magyar church, and no diet or sultan answered it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordinary sequence of sending, preaching, hearing and believing, which does not change with the political settlement. The Hungarian ministers who went down into the Ottoman plain were doing what is written, that “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4), and Karoli's Bible of 1590 answered the Pentecostal demand that men hear “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8). The kingdom was partitioned between two empires and the church was neither empire's, for “For the kingdom is the LORD'S” (Psa 22:28).

pos: n. (the principality beyond the forest, Reformed in its princes, and the first state in Europe to put religious toleration into statute)
etymology: Latin Transsilvania, the land beyond the forest; Hungarian Erdély; German Siebenbürgen, the seven fortresses.
biblical_def: Transylvania was an Ottoman tributary principality which, because it answered to a Muslim overlord rather than a Catholic emperor, became the one Reformed state in eastern Europe. Its Saxon towns adopted the Augsburg Confession in 1550, its Magyars the Helvetic, and its princes from Bocskai through Gabriel Bethlen to the Rakoczis were Reformed men who endowed colleges at Kolozsvar, Nagyenyed and Nagyvarad, imported Puritan and Dutch learning, and printed Hungarian Scripture and catechisms. The Diet of Torda in 1568 enacted that ministers should preach the gospel according to their own understanding and that no one should be harmed for his religion, which is the earliest such statute in Europe. It had a cost the dictionary does not hide: the same liberty admitted the antitrinitarian party of Giorgio Biandrata and Ferenc David, and Transylvania became the one country where Unitarianism was a legally received religion, placed by the law beside the churches that confess the Son. The Reformed synods fought it with argument and the princes eventually with the law. The dictionary enters Transylvania because it holds together, in one small country, the best and the worst that civil toleration produces: the Hungarian Reformed church was free to be built, and a denial of Christ was free to be established.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines toleration as the allowance by law of religious opinions; a principality as the territory of a prince; to deny as to contradict or disown; and liberty as freedom from restraint.
webster_full: TOLERATION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to or different from those of the established church.
PRINCIPALITY, n. Sovereignty; supreme power; the territory of a prince, or the country which gives title to a prince.
DENY, v. To contradict; to gainsay; to declare a statement or position not to be true; to disown.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit, without other restraint than the laws.
ENDOW, v. To furnish with a portion of estate; to settle a permanent provision upon, as a college or church.

corruption_summary: Ottoman tributary principality, Reformed in its princes, which enacted the Torda toleration of 1568 and thereby also established Unitarianism by law.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is Unitarianism, received as a lawful religion in Transylvania and nowhere else in Europe, and the dictionary names it by the apostle's own classification rather than as a variant opinion. Giorgio Biandrata and Ferenc David denied that the Son is God, and the first epistle of John settles what that is without any assistance from a synod. The toleration of 1568 was a civil law and the dictionary does not regret civil liberty; it records that civil liberty is not a doctrinal verdict, and that the Reformed synods of Transylvania were right to spend two generations arguing the point rather than treating it as settled by the statute.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that liberty to preach is not licence to preach anything, and that the congregation is the court of first instance. “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) is the standard by which the Torda liberty was to be used, and the Transylvanians who used it rightly are described in what is said of the Bereans, that they “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). To the Reformed church that held its ground among four received religions the word is “hold that fast which thou hast” (Rev 3:11).

pos: n. (the Hungarian market town on the great plain called the Calvinist Rome, seat of the confession of 1562 and the synod of 1567)
etymology: Hungarian Debrecen, perhaps from a Slavic or Turkic personal name; the town is first named in 1235.
biblical_def: Debrecen is the town that gave the Hungarian Reformed church its confession, its press and its college, and it did so under Ottoman overlordship with no prince to protect it. A cattle-market town on the treeless plain, it had no walls, no bishop and no university, and it turned Reformed in the 1550s under Martin Kalmancsehi and then Peter Melius, who was its minister from 1558 and the organiser of the Hungarian church. The Debrecen Confession of 1562, drawn up by Melius and Gergely Szegedi, set out the Reformed faith against both Rome and the antitrinitarians in Hungarian. The Synod of Debrecen in 1567 adopted the Second Helvetic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism, settled a presbyterian-synodical order, and fixed the doctrine of the Magyar church for four centuries. The town's press printed in Hungarian from 1561, its college trained the ministry and sent its best students to Wittenberg, Heidelberg, Franeker and Leiden, and Gyorgy Martonfalvi taught there against the Jesuits. It is called the Calvinist Rome because for three hundred years every Hungarian Reformed minister passed through it. The dictionary enters Debrecen because it shows a church fully furnished with the three things that outlast persecution: a confession, a press and a school.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; a catechism as a form of instruction by question and answer; a college as a society of men for the pursuit of learning; and a press as the business of printing.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an assembly of ministers and elders.
CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
COLLEGE, n. A society of men invested with certain powers, engaged in some common pursuit, chiefly of learning.
PRESS, n. A machine for printing; the art or business of printing and publishing.
MARKET, n. A public place in a city or town where provisions or cattle are exposed for sale; the rate of purchase and sale.
scriptures: Neh 8:8

Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Act 16:5
And so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily.
corruption_summary: Hungarian market town on the plain, Reformed from the 1550s, which produced the Confession of 1562 and the Synod of 1567 and trained the Magyar ministry.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the revival that leaves nothing behind, and Debrecen is the reproof of it. Hungary in the 1550s was full of preaching and short of order; what Melius added was a confession in the vernacular, a printed catechism, a synod that could meet and decide, and a college that examined the men it sent out. None of that is glamorous and all of it is what survived the Jesuits, the Habsburg commissions and the Decade of Mourning. “And when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) is the apostolic pattern, and the pattern is unexciting on purpose.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is teaching that aims at understanding rather than at impression. “and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) is the whole programme of the Debrecen press and the Debrecen college, and a minister trained there was expected to be “a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15). The result is what is recorded of the churches of Asia, that “so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily” (Act 16:5).

pos: n. (the Orthodox principality east of the Carpathians, where the Synod of Jassy in 1642 condemned a confession of Reformed doctrine)
etymology: Latin Moldavia, from the river Moldova; Romanian Moldova; the principality dates from the fourteenth century.
biblical_def: Moldavia is the Orthodox principality in which the Reformation was examined from the outside and formally rejected. Hungarian settlers in its eastern districts had been reached by Hussite preaching in the fifteenth century, and Reformed and Lutheran congregations of Magyars and Saxons existed there under the princes' sufferance. The event that puts Moldavia in a Reformed dictionary is the Synod of Jassy, held in its capital in 1642 under Prince Vasile Lupu and the metropolitan Varlaam, which examined and condemned the confession published in 1629 under the name of Cyril Lucaris, patriarch of Constantinople, a document that taught election, justification by faith, the authority of Scripture over tradition and the reception of two sacraments. Jassy condemned it, Peter Mogila's orthodox confession was prepared as the answer, and Jerusalem confirmed the condemnation ten years later. The dictionary enters Moldavia because the Lucaris confession is the one serious attempt to carry Reformation doctrine into the Greek church, and Jassy is where it was refused. What the eastern church preserved is genuine and is honoured here: the Trinity and the person of Christ as Nicaea and Chalcedon confessed them. What it refused at Jassy is justification by faith alone and the supremacy of Scripture over tradition, and that refusal is what the dictionary records.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a patriarch as a dignitary superior to an archbishop; a metropolitan as a bishop having authority over other bishops; to condemn as to pronounce to be wrong; and tradition as the delivery of opinions by oral communication.
webster_full: PATRIARCH, n. In the Christian church, a dignitary superior to the order of archbishops.
METROPOLITAN, n. A bishop who presides over other bishops; an archbishop having authority over a province.
CONDEMN, v. To pronounce to be utterly wrong; to censure; to pass sentence upon.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, by oral communication.
CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; an avowal of belief.

corruption_summary: Orthodox principality east of the Carpathians whose Synod of Jassy in 1642 condemned the Reformed confession published under the name of Cyril Lucaris.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the elevation of tradition to the level of Scripture, which is what the Synod of Jassy defended and the Lucaris confession had denied. The dictionary honours what the eastern church kept when the West was corrupting it: Nicene Trinitarianism and Chalcedonian Christology, held without the papal monarchy. It names what Jassy refused: that Scripture is the judge of tradition and not its peer, and that a sinner is justified by faith without the works of the law. On the first point the standard is plain, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), and a tradition that claims equal inspiration claims what no tradition has.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an appeal to antiquity is answered from the text, not from an older council. “Search the scriptures” (Joh 5:39) was said to men who had the whole weight of tradition on their side and had missed the Christ it testified of. Moldavia also shows the dictionary's own duty of fairness: Lucaris was a Greek patriarch, not a Dutch professor, and the confession under his name was condemned by his own communion. The right response to that is argument from the text, and “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) is where the argument must be made.

pos: n. (the Orthodox principality between the Carpathians and the Danube, where Lutheran patronage produced the first printed Scripture in Romanian)
etymology: Latin Valachia, from the Germanic Walh, a Roman or Latin-speaker; Romanian Ţara Românească, the Romanian land.
biblical_def: Wallachia is the principality through which the Reformation gave the Romanians their first printed books in their own language, without ever gaining a congregation there. The Romanian church used Church Slavonic in its services, a tongue the people did not speak, and the Reformation's principle of worship in the vernacular struck directly at that. The Lutheran Saxon council of Brasov in Transylvania, with the Wallachian princes' permission and sometimes their money, employed the deacon Coresi, who between 1559 and 1581 printed in Romanian a catechism, a Gospel book, the Acts, a Psalter and a book of homilies, carrying his press between Brasov and Targoviste. Coresi was an Orthodox deacon working for Lutheran patrons, and his prefaces argue the Reformation case plainly: that a people should hear the word in the speech they were born in, since a priest who speaks in an unknown tongue is a pipe without a note. No Reformed church took root in Wallachia and the liturgy stayed Slavonic for another century. What remained was the printed Romanian word, and the modern Romanian Bible descends from that work. The dictionary enters Wallachia because it shows the Reformation's vernacular principle doing good far outside the Reformation's borders.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vernacular as native, belonging to the country of one's birth; a psalter as the book of Psalms; a homily as a discourse read to a congregation; and a deacon as a minister in the lowest degree of holy orders.
webster_full: VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
PSALTER, n. The book of Psalms; often applied to a book containing the Psalms separately printed.
HOMILY, n. A discourse or sermon read or pronounced to an audience; a plain familiar discourse on a religious subject.
DEACON, n. A person in the lowest degree of holy orders; an officer in the Christian church.
PIPE, n. A wind instrument of music; a tube of wood or metal used in the organ.

Neh 8:8

corruption_summary: Orthodox principality on the Danube where the deacon Coresi, patronised by Lutheran Brasov, printed the first Romanian Scripture between 1559 and 1581.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is worship in an unknown tongue, and Wallachia is where the Reformation answered it in a church it never entered. Church Slavonic was a dead language to Romanian peasants, and the argument for keeping it was the argument always made: that the sacred language is holier than the common one. The apostle settles it with a figure a ploughman can follow: “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9). Coresi's prefaces make the same case in Romanian, and a Lutheran town council paid for them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the goal of public worship is understanding, and that this is a point of charity rather than of taste. “I had rather speak five words with my understanding” (1Co 14:19) is the apostle's own preference, and it is the whole case for the vernacular Bible. What Wallachia proves is that the principle outruns the party which holds it: no Reformed congregation was planted there, and yet a nation received its Scripture in its own speech because men who believed “caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) paid a printer to do it.

pos: n. (the eastern Slavic lands of the Polish-Lithuanian commonwealth, where the Union of Brest in 1596 divided the Orthodox from themselves)
etymology: Latin Ruthenia, a medieval rendering of Rus; the name covers the Orthodox Slavs of the commonwealth, Ukrainian and Belarusian.
biblical_def: Ruthenia is the name the Latin West gave to the Orthodox Slavs of the Polish-Lithuanian commonwealth, and its sixteenth century is a case study in what happens to a church whose people cannot read its services. The liturgy was in Church Slavonic, the bishops were appointed by the crown out of the nobility and frequently illiterate in theology, and the Reformation reached the Ruthenian nobility first, many of whom became Reformed or antitrinitarian and some of whom then returned to Rome. The answer came from two directions. Lay brotherhoods in Lviv, Vilnius and other towns took up the printing of Slavonic books, the running of schools and the discipline of their own clergy, in effect a lay reformation inside Orthodoxy; and in 1596 a majority of the Ruthenian bishops, at Brest, submitted to the pope while keeping the eastern rite, creating the Uniate church and splitting the Ruthenian people in two. The brotherhoods and a remnant of bishops refused, and the quarrel ran for centuries. The dictionary enters Ruthenia because the Union of Brest is the clearest instance of a reform that addressed the hierarchy and left the people exactly where they were: the same unread liturgy, now under a different jurisdiction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a brotherhood as an association of men for any purpose; a union as the act of joining into one; a rite as an external ceremony of religion; and jurisdiction as legal authority or extent of power.
webster_full: BROTHERHOOD, n. An association of men for any purpose, as a society of monks; a class of men of the same occupation.
UNION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one; concord; agreement and conjunction of mind, will and affections.
RITE, n. The manner of performing divine or solemn service; an external ceremony or observance in religion.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the limit within which power may be exercised.
LAITY, n. The people, as distinguished from the clergy; the body of the people not in orders.

corruption_summary: The Orthodox Slavic lands of the Polish-Lithuanian commonwealth, where lay brotherhoods printed and taught and the Union of Brest in 1596 divided the people.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the reform that changes the jurisdiction and leaves the pulpit alone. Brest moved the Ruthenian hierarchy from Constantinople to Rome, kept the eastern rite and the Slavonic liturgy untouched, and gave the ploughman of Volhynia nothing he could understand that he had not had before. The Reformation's question was the other one: “how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9). Where Ruthenia came nearest to answering it was in the brotherhoods, laymen who bought presses and opened schools because their bishops would not.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the first duty of a shepherd is to feed, and that a shepherd who cannot is under a woe whatever his see. “Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture” (Jer 23:1) is addressed to men holding a lawful office. Against it stands the plain apostolic standard of a people who, having the text, “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11), and the Ruthenian brotherhoods were the nearest thing their church had to it.

pos: n. (the Ruthenian province of the commonwealth, seat of Ostrog, where the first complete printed Slavonic Bible was produced in 1581)
etymology: Latin Volhynia, from the old town of Volyn on the Bug; Polish Wołyń, Ukrainian Volyn.
biblical_def: Volhynia is the province in which a great Orthodox magnate did for his own church what the Reformation was doing in the West, and where the same liberty produced the sharpest denial of Christ in Europe. Prince Konstanty Wasyl Ostrogski, the richest man in the commonwealth, founded at Ostrog about 1576 a school with Greek and Latin, gathered scholars, set up a press, and in 1581 printed the Ostrog Bible, the first complete Bible in Church Slavonic ever to be printed, collated from Greek and Slavonic manuscripts and furnished with prefaces. He refused the Union of Brest and died Orthodox. At the same time Volhynia, under the religious liberty of the Warsaw Confederation of 1573, filled with congregations of the Polish Brethren, the antitrinitarian body which denied the deity of the Son and the satisfaction of the cross, sheltered by Reformed and Orthodox nobles alike as a matter of noble privilege. The dictionary enters Volhynia because the two things happened in one province within one generation: a Bible printed for a people who had never had one, and a doctrine printed that emptied the Bible of its Christ, and the second was protected by the same liberty as the first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a magnate as a person of rank or great influence; collation as the comparing of copies; a privilege as a peculiar advantage enjoyed by a person or class; and satisfaction as that which fully answers a claim.
webster_full: MAGNATE, n. A person of rank; a grandee or noble; a man of great power or influence.
COLLATION, n. The act of comparing one thing with another, as copies of a book or manuscript.
PRIVILEGE, n. A particular and peculiar benefit or advantage enjoyed by a person, company or society, beyond the common advantages of other citizens.
SATISFACTION, n. That which satisfies; payment; atonement for a crime; the payment of a debt or a penalty.
PRESS, n. A machine for printing; the art or business of printing and publishing.
scriptures: Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
Act 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Rev 3:11
Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.
corruption_summary: Ruthenian province of the commonwealth where Prince Ostrogski printed the first complete Slavonic Bible in 1581 and the Polish Brethren were sheltered by noble privilege.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is antitrinitarianism, and Volhynia is where it enjoyed the most comfortable protection it ever had. The Polish Brethren taught that the Son is not God and that the cross is an example rather than a satisfaction, and they taught it under the Warsaw Confederation of 1573 with great nobles as patrons. The dictionary names the doctrine for what it is and names also what made it possible: a liberty held as the private right of a landowner, in which a congregation's doctrine depended on which lord owned the village. “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) is the test, and a patron's pleasure is not it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture given to a people in their own speech is the instrument that corrects them, which is why the Ostrog press was a greater service to Volhynia than any nobleman's protection. “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7) is the ground of every such labour. The Ostrog Bible also answers the objection that the eastern church had no translators: it had one magnate who paid for it, and the men of Pentecost heard “in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11), which is the warrant he worked on.

pos: n. (the south-eastern frontier province of the commonwealth, where a church of noble patrons was swept away by war and left almost nothing)
etymology: Latin Podolia, from the Slavic po dolu, along the lowland or valley; Polish Podole, Ukrainian Podillia.
biblical_def: Podolia is the frontier province where the Polish Reformation was planted entirely on noble estates and entirely disappeared. It lay between the commonwealth and the Tatar steppe, a land of fortified towns, Ruthenian peasants and Polish landlords, and after the Warsaw Confederation of 1573 those landlords did as landlords did elsewhere in the commonwealth: some settled Reformed ministers in their villages, others settled Brethren of the antitrinitarian party, and the peasantry followed whichever had the estate. There was no synodical structure of consequence, no press, no college, and no Ruthenian-speaking ministry, so nothing was built that a change of landlord could not undo. The seventeenth century undid it completely. Tatar raiding, the Cossack rising of 1648, the Muscovite and Ottoman wars, and the expulsion of the Polish Brethren from the commonwealth in 1658 together removed patrons, ministers and congregations, and the Catholic and Uniate settlement that followed found no Protestant body to resist it. The dictionary enters Podolia as the negative case beside Debrecen: the same century, the same legal toleration, and the opposite result, because one province built a confession, a press and a school and the other built none.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a frontier as the border of a country; a patron as a protector or supporter; a plantation as the place planted or settled; and desolation as a laying waste or destruction.
webster_full: FRONTIER, n. The marches; the border, confine or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
PATRON, n. A protector; a supporter; one who countenances, supports or protects.
PLANTATION, n. The act of planting or setting in the earth; the place planted; a colony or settlement.
DESOLATION, n. The act of desolating; destruction; a laying waste; a place deprived of inhabitants.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that upon which anything stands and by which it is supported.
scriptures: Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation:
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
corruption_summary: South-eastern frontier province of the commonwealth, Protestant only on noble estates, and swept away without remainder by the wars from 1648.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the church planted as an estate improvement, which is what much of the Polish Reformation was in its frontier provinces. A lord settled a minister as he settled a miller, the villagers conformed to the manor, and when the manor changed hands or burned, the congregation ended. The apostolic concern was the opposite, to lay a foundation that would stand without the founder: “lest I should build upon another man's foundation” (Rom 15:20). Podolia had no foundation of its own at all, and the war of 1648 proved it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordaining of a settled ministry in every congregation, which is the only thing that makes a church outlast its patron. “And when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) is what Podolia never did and Debrecen did. The province is a sober commentary on the rule that “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7), and on the reminder that the planter and the waterer are nothing, for “God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6).

pos: n. (the Habsburg-Ottoman borderland whose Protestant press at Urach printed Scripture in Glagolitic and Cyrillic for the South Slavs)
etymology: Latin Croatia, from the Slavic Hrvat, a Croat; Croatian Hrvatska.
biblical_def: Croatia is the land for which the most ambitious translation project of the Reformation was undertaken, and in which almost none of it could be delivered. Croatia and its Dalmatian and Istrian coast lay on the Ottoman frontier, raided, divided and largely without schools, and its people used Glagolitic and Cyrillic letters as well as Latin. Hans Ungnad of Sonnegg, a Styrian nobleman who had gone into exile for the gospel, set up at Urach near Tubingen in 1561 a South Slavic press at his own cost, under Primoz Trubar's general direction, with Stipan Konzul of Istria and Antun Dalmatin as translators and Pietro Paolo Vergerio among its promoters. Within three years it printed some thirty titles, including the New Testament in Croatian in both Glagolitic and Cyrillic type, a catechism, a postil and the Augsburg Confession, and the Cyrillic books were intended to reach Serbs and the Christians under Ottoman rule. Ungnad died in 1564, the money stopped, the frontier was impassable, and the books were distributed only in part. The dictionary enters Croatia because the Urach press is the Reformation at its most self-forgetful: a dying exile spending his estate to print Scripture in two alphabets for a people he would never see.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an alphabet as the letters of a language arranged in order; a type as a printing letter; an exile as one banished from his country; and a postil as a short exposition of the gospel.
webster_full: ALPHABET, n. The letters of a language arranged in the customary order; the series of letters which form the elements of speech.
TYPE, n. A printing letter; the letters and characters used by printers; a stamp or emblem.
EXILE, n. One who is banished from his own country, or who abandons it for his own safety.
POSTIL, n. A marginal note; a short exposition or homily upon the gospel of the day.
BORDER, n. The outer edge of anything; the exterior limit of a country or region; a frontier.
scriptures: Act 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Rev 14:6
And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
corruption_summary: Habsburg-Ottoman borderland for which the Urach press, funded by the exile Hans Ungnad from 1561, printed Scripture in Glagolitic and Cyrillic.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the calculation that counts a labour wasted because its results cannot be measured. By any such reckoning Urach failed: Ungnad spent an estate, died in three years, and most of the books never reached the Croats or the Serbs they were cut for. The dictionary declines the reckoning. The command is to go and teach, and the promise attached to the labour is not a percentage of distribution: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58). The Croatian and Serbian letters existed in print, and that was not undone by the frontier.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that translation is obedience to a command and not an investment. “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) is addressed to men with no press at all, and the everlasting gospel is to be preached “to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” (Rev 14:6), which is a list that includes peoples on the far side of an impassable border. Urach's two alphabets are the exact shape of that obedience in 1561.

pos: n. (the Slovene duchy about Ljubljana, where Primoz Trubar made a literary language and Jurij Dalmatin completed the Slovene Bible in 1584)
etymology: Latin Carniola, German Krain, Slovene Kranjska, from the Slavic krajina, a march or borderland.
biblical_def: Carniola is the duchy in which the Reformation made a nation a language and then lost the nation. The Slovenes of Carniola, Styria and Carinthia had no printed books in their speech at all when Primoz Trubar, a priest of Ljubljana driven into exile in 1548, published at Tubingen in 1550 a catechism and a primer in Slovene, the first books ever printed in that tongue. He followed them with the New Testament between 1555 and 1577, a hymnal, and a church order; Jurij Dalmatin completed the whole Bible in Slovene, printed at Wittenberg in 1584; and Adam Bohoric published a Slovene grammar in the same year. Carniola's estates were largely Lutheran, Ljubljana had an evangelical school and a consistory, and for a generation the duchy was a Protestant country. Then Ferdinand's reformation commissions came through after 1598 by the Styrian method: preachers expelled, the school closed, books collected and publicly burned at Ljubljana, the nobility required to conform or sell. Protestant Carniola ended. The Bible did not: Dalmatin's version was read in secret, and Catholic Slovene writing afterwards had to build on the literary language the Reformation had made. The dictionary enters Carniola because it shows what survives a thorough suppression, which is the Bible and the speech it was put into.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a primer as a small elementary book for teaching children; a grammar as the art of speaking and writing a language correctly; to suppress as to crush or put an end to; and a consistory as an ecclesiastical court or assembly.
webster_full: PRIMER, n. A small elementary book for religious instruction, or for teaching children to read.
GRAMMAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; a system of general principles of a language.
SUPPRESS, v. To crush; to subdue; to put an end to; to destroy; to conceal from the public.
CONSISTORY, n. A place of justice in a spiritual court; an assembly of ecclesiastical persons; a church session.
TONGUE, n. The language spoken by a particular nation; speech; the power of speaking.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
But the word of the Lord endureth for ever. And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you.
Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
corruption_summary: Slovene duchy about Ljubljana, Lutheran under its estates, where Trubar printed the first Slovene books from 1550 and Dalmatin the whole Bible in 1584.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the confidence that a book can be ended by burning it, which the commissioners at Ljubljana acted on and which Carniola refutes. The preachers were expelled, the school was shut, the nobility was bought out or driven out, and the Protestant books of the duchy were heaped and burned in public; by every political measure the work of fifty years was cancelled. Dalmatin's Bible went on being read in farmhouses, and the Slovene that Trubar had standardised went on being the only written Slovene there was. “the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) is not a figure of speech.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a translation serves generations that will not share the translator's confession, and is not thereby wasted. Catholic Slovene writers after 1600 had to use the literary language the Reformation had made, so that Trubar's labour outlived Trubar's church in his own country. “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mat 24:35) is the ground of it, and the Pentecostal question “how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8) is what the Slovene New Testament of 1555 answered for a people of half a million.
